query: For as-deposited, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type high-entropy alloys intended for magnetic refrigeration, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their magnetocaloric response and hysteresis during low-applied-field magnetic-cooling cycles? Earlier work focused mainly on arc-melted ingots and melt-spun microribbons, where an ordered single-phase hexagonal state undergoes a first-order magnetostructural transition that produces a large but sharp and hysteretic entropy change; these bulk forms also have limited heat-exchange rates because of their low surface-to-volume ratio. Prior searches have largely emphasized composition-dependent changes in transition temperature or response amplitude, with most studies pursuing only one optimization variable. Under the constraints of avoiding rare-earth elements, retaining mechanical stability and low cost, enabling rapid heat exchange, and limiting hysteretic losses, specify one controlled intervention that would distinguish the proposed governing explanation from alternatives, the predicted observations relative to the as-deposited baseline, the boundaries over which those predictions should hold, the prior observations that support the hypothesis, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In as-deposited, non-equiatomic Fe–Mn–Ni–Ge–Si high-entropy alloys that are hexagonal (Ni2In-type) at ambient conditions, the magnetocaloric response and hysteresis under low applied fields are governed primarily by the density of transformation-accommodating interfaces (grain and twin boundaries) and the associated elastic/chemical heterogeneity they introduce. Higher interfacial density and residual microstrain lower the nucleation barrier and distribute local transition temperatures, broadening the first-order magnetostructural transition, reducing magnetic/thermal hysteresis losses, and increasing low-field relative cooling power despite a reduced peak entropy change. This interfacial-control mechanism, not composition alone, sets the shape and losses of the low-field response in the as-deposited state.
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited nanocrystalline Fe–Mn–Ni–Ge–Si alloy thin film or foil (single-phase hexagonal Ni2In-type austenite at room temperature), non-equiatomic but fixed composition across samples, with residual microstrain from deposition and a grain size on the order of 50–300 nm, showing a first-order magnetostructural transition near the target operating temperature with measurable hysteresis.
generation.intervention: At fixed composition, vary interfacial density by producing a controlled series of deposits with different grain sizes via substrate temperature during sputter deposition (e.g., 200, 350, 500 °C) or brief low-temperature anneals that adjust grain size 30–300 nm without changing phase or composition. Alternatively, introduce a nanolaminate (e.g., periodic 5–20 nm-thick alloy layers separated by 1–3 nm inert spacers) to increase interface density while keeping the alloy chemistry constant.
generation.conditions: Low applied magnetic fields ≤1 T, cycling around the transition temperature at rates relevant to magnetic cooling (e.g., 0.05–0.5 K/s thermal sweep, 0.1–1 Hz field cycles), ambient pressure, and film/foil thickness ≤10 μm to enable rapid heat exchange. Measurements near the transition within ±60 K of the as-deposited transition temperature.
generation.structural_mediator: Interfacial density and character: grain boundary area per unit volume, twin boundary density, and associated residual microstrain and chemical short-range order fluctuations that create a distribution of local martensitic start/finish temperatures.
generation.mechanism: Interfaces and their elastic fields reduce the nucleation barrier for the hexagonal-to-martensitic transformation and permit multivariant growth with better strain accommodation, lowering dissipative hysteresis. Concurrently, spatial variations in local composition and microstrain near interfaces broaden the distribution of transition temperatures, smoothing the first-order transition under low fields. The net effect is reduced hysteresis area and a broader but lower peak ΔS(T), improving low-field relative cooling power.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the as-deposited baseline at fixed composition: (a) decreasing grain size from ~200–300 nm to ~30–60 nm (or introducing a high-density nanolaminate) will reduce magnetic hysteresis energy loss per cycle at H_max = 1 T by roughly 30–60% and reduce thermal hysteresis width ΔT_hyst by ~25–50%; (b) the ΔS_peak(T; 0→1 T) will decrease by ~20–40% while its temperature full-width-at-half-maximum will increase by ~50–100%, yielding a relative cooling power that is unchanged to moderately higher (+10–30%); (c) latent heat measured by DSC will be distributed over a wider T-range with a modest reduction in peak but similar integrated area within measurement uncertainty; (d) XRD peak widths and Williamson–Hall analysis will show increased microstrain for higher interfacial density samples, correlating with reduced hysteresis.
generation.baseline: As-deposited, single-layer film/foil with grain size ~150–250 nm, showing a sharp first-order transition with large ΔS_peak but substantial hysteresis (magnetic loop area and ΔT_hyst), and a relatively narrow ΔS(T) peak under ≤1 T.
generation.boundary: Predictions apply for: (i) samples retaining single-phase hexagonal Ni2In-type austenite at room temperature and a reversible magnetostructural transition; (ii) grain sizes ~20–300 nm (below ~10–15 nm, loss of long-range order may suppress the first-order transition; above ~300 nm, interfacial effects weaken); (iii) low applied fields ≤1 T (at ≥3 T, field-dominated kinetics may mask microstructural control); (iv) compositions within the Fe–Mn–Ni–Ge–Si window that avoid multiphase separation. Strong substrate clamping or formation of secondary phases invalidates the expected trends.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative effect sizes depend on the residual stress state, texture, and defect chemistry introduced by the specific deposition conditions; excessive interfacial disorder could over-broaden the transition and reduce RCP. The balance between reduced hysteresis and decreased ΔS_peak may vary with thickness and thermal boundary conditions. Twin vs. grain boundary dominance may differ across processing routes.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare at least four samples at identical Fe–Mn–Ni–Ge–Si composition (verified by ICP/OES or XRF) with systematically varied grain size/interfacial density: two single-layer films/foils deposited at low vs. high substrate temperature to target ~50 nm and ~200 nm grains, one briefly annealed to coarsen to ~300 nm, and one nanolaminate to maximize interface density. Confirm single-phase hexagonal structure at room temperature. Measure grain size (TEM, EBSD, XRD line broadening), microstrain (Williamson–Hall or synchrotron XRD), and twin boundary density (TEM). Acquire M–T under 0.5 and 1 T with heating/cooling cycles to extract ΔS(T) via Maxwell relation and thermal hysteresis; measure DSC for latent heat distribution; record quasi-static M–H loops up to 1 T around the transition to quantify hysteresis energy per cycle. Keep thickness and thermal environment constant across samples.
measurements: Grain size distribution (TEM/EBSD), grain boundary area density
M–T and ΔS(T) under 0.5–1 T; ΔS_peak and FWHM
Magnetic hysteresis energy per cycle from M–H loops at 0.5–1 T
Thermal hysteresis width ΔT_hyst from heating/cooling cycles
DSC latent heat vs. temperature profile
Relative cooling power (ΔS_peak × FWHM) under 0.5–1 T
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: At fixed composition, if doubling the grain boundary area density (e.g., roughly halving the average grain size) does not reduce the magnetic hysteresis energy per cycle at H_max = 1 T by at least 20% and does not increase the ΔS(T) FWHM by at least 25%, or if changes show no monotonic correlation with interfacial density/microstrain, then the hypothesis is falsified.
